newsitem.title: GERMANY: Yeltsin in Germany for spa-town talks with Kohl.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin in Germany for spa-town talks with Kohl.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin began a visit to Germany on Wednesday that will include talks with Chancellor Helmut Kohl likely to focus on the vexed question of Moscow's hostility to NATO expansion.

The Russian leader's official intinerary is packed into Thursday and he is scheduled to leave for home early on Friday morning. He is due to receive a "Man of the Year" award from the German media at a ceremony attended by Kohl on Thursday night.

Yeltsin, who has bounced back from major heart surgery and pneumonia in the last five months, smiled and waved briefly as he and his wife Naina stepped off his newly fitted-out presidential jet at Stuttgart airport in southern Germany.
He reviewed an honour guard of German police, but declined to make any comment to waiting reporters.

Despite having arrived in the home city of luxury carmaker Mercedes-Benz, Yeltsin, who this week launched a "Buy Russian" campaign at home amid much fanfare, stepped into a Russian ZiL limousine for the 70-km (45-mile) drive to Baden-Baden.
Kohl was scheduled to welcome the president with full military honours on Thursday in the elegant spa town at the start of Yeltsin's public programme.

The talks between the two leaders, their second meeting in three months, were likely to focus on intensive efforts to negotiate a charter to give Russia a say in the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation as the alliance prepares to take in members from the former Soviet bloc in eastern Europe.

NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov failed to iron out differences in Moscow on Tuesday, and presidential spokesman Sergey Yastrzhembsky said Kohl and Yeltsin could play a key role.
"It seems to me that the German chancellor is one of those Western politicians who are more sensitive to Russian arguments," he told Russian television on Tuesday.
"...The chancellor's opinion is of particular importance, since I think the chancellor can speak very tellingly to his NATO partners after hearing the president's point of view."
Whenever the two men meet, there is hope in Western capitals that Kohl, Russia's biggest advocate in the West, can use his warm personal ties with Yeltsin to ease strains with Moscow.

But even that friendship has failed to end a row over the vast collection of art shipped out of occupied Germany by the Soviet army as "war booty" at the end of World War Two, including golden treasure from ancient Troy.

Russia's upper house of parliament on Wednesday delayed a vote to overrule a veto from Yeltsin and declare the art Russia's property. Deputies said Yeltsin had urged the chamber not to pass the vote while he was in Germany.

There was some puzzlement in Germany over comments by Yeltsin, who told the weekly magazine Stern he would have some of the treasures in his luggage when he came. "Not the Troy gold of course," he said. "But I'll bring some other items with me."
Baden-Baden, a spa since Roman times, had its heyday as a society resort in the 19th century.
Tsar Alexander II visited in 1863, as did many other crowned heads and nobility drawn by the waters and the famous casino, the setting of Fyodor Dostoyevsky's novel The Gambler.

Yeltsin was staying in a luxury 19th century hotel with a river running through the grounds. Its plush apartments cost $1,500 a night and and it occasionally welcomes some of Russia's post-communist newly rich.
Yeltsin is due to receive the "Man of the Year" prize for 1996 on Thursday night and Kohl is scheduled to make a speech in praise of his friend.
Amid the pomp, two groups said they planned protests in Baden-Baden against alleged human rights abuse in Russia.
Amnesty International said it would urge Yeltsin to do more to protect critical journalists, of whom several had been killed or disappeared while reporting on the conflict in Chechnya.

And the Society for Threatened Peoples said the media award had tastelessly cast Yeltsin in a positive light only weeks after the end of the bloody conflict with Chechen rebels for which he shared responsibility.
